extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, geologists, systematists, and educated readers interested in evolutionary theory
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and lines of evidence for judging the adequacy of the theory of descent with modification (natural selection), as presented by Darwin: what observations, patterns, and explanatory virtues a satisfactory account of species origin should meet. Useful for assessing evolutionary hypotheses and the weight of supporting or opposing data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imperfection of the geological record
rubrics_metrics.description: The geological record is imperfect to a degree that we should not expect to find most intermediate links; formations are intermittently accumulated and many classes are rarely preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of intermediate fossils is not decisive against descent; explanations include limited temporal and spatial sampling, intermittent deposition, selective preservation, local varieties appearing suddenly in formations, and huge blank intervals between formations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of time for gradual change
rubrics_metrics.description: There has been a lapse of time so great as to be utterly inappreciable by the human intellect, allowing countless generations for slow change to accumulate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long duration justifies expectation of slow, graduated modification; apparent suddenness in the fossil record can result from the record's incompleteness rather than rapid creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observed variability under domestication
rubrics_metrics.description: Under domestication we see much variability; the reproductive system is eminently susceptible to changes in conditions of life, and modifications can be inherited for long periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Domesticated breeds demonstrate that small, cumulative selection of naturally arising variations can produce large results; man’s selection is analogous to natural selection and shows heritability and accumulative change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of natural variability and varieties
rubrics_metrics.description: All naturalists have admitted the existence of varieties which are often indistinguishable in kind from species; no clear distinction can be drawn between individual differences, slight varieties, sub-species, and species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If species and varieties form a continuum, the existence of intermediate and incipient forms favors descent; taxonomic rank alone is not reliable to separate created species from modified varieties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Struggle for existence (overproduction and competition)
rubrics_metrics.description: More individuals are born than can possibly survive; the high geometrical ratio of increase results in a struggle for existence in which the slightest advantage determines survival and reproductive success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any theory must account for overproduction and competitive selection pressures; such pressures provide the mechanism by which advantageous variations are preserved and accumulated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural selection accumulates slight successive favorable variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural selection acts solely by accumulating slight, successive, favourable variations and thus can produce no great or sudden modification but only short and slow steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanations invoking large, sudden changes (saltations) are unnecessary; the canon 'Natura non facit saltum' supports gradualism as a methodological expectation for evolutionary change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple causes of variability (correlation, use/disuse, physical conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Variability is governed by many complex laws — correlation of growth, by use and disuse, and by the direct action of physical conditions of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating causes of trait change, consider correlated responses, effects of use/disuse, and environment; natural selection operates in concert with these factors rather than alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heritability and persistence of modifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Modifications can be inherited for long periods; as long as conditions remain similar, an inherited modification may persist for an almost infinite number of generations though variability does not wholly cease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess claims of evolutionary change for evidence of heritability across many generations and for persistence under stable conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlation of classification and descent (natural system as genealogical)
rubrics_metrics.description: The natural system (classification with groups subordinate to groups) is intelligible as a genealogical arrangement due to inheritance or community of descent; embryological and rudimentary characters often have high classificatory value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A satisfactory theory should explain why classification groups exist, why adaptive characters are less reliable for classification, and why embryological and rudimentary traits reveal deep affinities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Homology and common structural patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarity of underlying structures (e.g., same framework of bones in man, bat, porpoise, horse) is explained by descent with modification from common progenitors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret homologous structures as evidence of common ancestry rather than independent special creation; explanatory frameworks should account for pattern reuse across diverse functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rudimentary organs as evidence of past function
rubrics_metrics.description: Rudimentary organs and organs useless in the adult (or present) state indicate inheritance from ancestors in which they were useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of apparently inutility-bearing parts (e.g., embryonic teeth, shrivelled wings) supports modification from ancestors and argues against special creation unless creationists can explain such inefficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embryological similarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Embryos of mammals, birds, reptiles, and fishes are closely alike, often displaying features like branchial slits and arterial loops similar to fish embryos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embryological resemblance at comparable stages supports common descent and developmental timing explanations (inheritance of traits expressed at corresponding ages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Biogeographical patterns and migration explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographical distribution (including island endemism, parallels between areas, and affinities to nearest mainlands) is intelligible by descent combined with past migrations and dispersal events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theory should explain why oceanic islands have few but often peculiar species, why some taxa are absent on islands (e.g., frogs), and why related species cluster near possible sources of immigrants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fossil succession and intermediacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Fossils from consecutive formations are more closely related to each other than those widely separated in time; fossils often stand intermediate between older and newer groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A robust evolutionary account predicts graded fossil sequences, intermediate forms (subject to incompleteness of record), and progressive divergence consistent with descent from common ancestors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extinction and replacement as expected outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Extinction of species and whole groups is almost inevitable under natural selection, as new and improved forms supplant older ones; neither species nor groups reappear after ordinary generation is broken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models should incorporate extinction dynamics and explain how replacement and continental persistence of allied forms arise from competition, modification, and dispersal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divergence of character and enlargement of successful groups
rubrics_metrics.description: Dominant species in large groups tend to give birth to new dominant and divergent forms; groups tend to increase in size and diverge in character, while less dominant groups may go extinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanations should account for unequal success among lineages, clustering of species within genera, and why some lineages radiate extensively while others remain small or vanish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instincts can be explained by gradual selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Marvellous instincts are no greater difficulty than bodily structure; instincts can be acquired slowly by natural selection, and habit is not indispensable (illustrated by neuter insects).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate behavioral traits for plausible stepwise adaptive histories; demonstrations that complex instinctual behaviors can be advantageous in intermediate forms strengthen evolutionary explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific characters more variable than generic characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific characters (those distinguishing species within a genus) tend to be more variable than generic characters; this is intelligible if species have diverged from a common progenitor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing character variability, expect traits that have changed recently (specific characters) to show more variation than deeply conserved generic traits; this pattern supports branching descent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversions and retained ancestral traits
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversions to long-lost characters occur (e.g., stripes appearing in horse species and hybrids), indicating descent from ancestors bearing these characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occurrences of atavisms or re-expressed ancestral traits are interpretable as retention of underlying hereditary capacity and favor historical/decent-based explanations over independent creation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory scope: account for apparent maladaptations
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory should explain why many contrivances are not absolutely perfect and why some apparently maladaptive features (sting causing bee's death, drones, waste of pollen, parasitism) exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A good evolutionary account must tolerate and explain suboptimal or wasteful traits as by-products of selection under ecological constraints, life-history trade-offs, or historical contingency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy and biochemical/cellular commonalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogy (shared chemical composition, cell structure, germinal vesicles, growth laws) suggests common origin; similar poisons affecting both plants and animals and similar developmental phenomena point to unity of plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate macro-level hypotheses against micro-level biochemical and cellular similarities: shared basic chemistry and cell structure provide independent lines of support for common ancestry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical consequence for taxonomy (weighing amount of difference)
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematists should weigh the actual amount of difference between forms more carefully; the distinction between species and well-marked varieties is that varieties are currently connected by intermediate gradations while species were formerly so connected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taxonomic decisions should prioritize degree and constancy of difference and seek intermediate gradations; the focus should shift from rigid categorical labels to evaluating continuity and magnitude of differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical standard for opponents: demand full explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Opponents who reject mutability demand full explanations of difficulties from proponents but often ignore deep unanswered questions on their own side (e.g., first appearance of species under creation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fair evaluation requires both critics and proponents to account for anomalies; burden of explanation should be symmetric and require specifying mechanisms rather than restating labels like 'plan of creation'.
